name: Horse oil
lead: Horse oil (ma-yu in Japanese and Korean cosmetic usage) is a fat rendered from horse tissue, traditionally from neck or mane fat, and used as an emollient in creams, balms and patches, particularly in East Asia. People use it to soften and moisturise skin and to support the skin barrier, which shows up as smoother, more supple-looking skin. Its fatty-acid profile, including linoleic and palmitoleic acids, has been described as similar to that of human skin lipids.[1]

Published work includes a small clinical evaluation of horse-oil microneedle patches in Korea, cell studies on UVB and inflammatory stress in keratinocytes, a mouse study, and formulation and analytical chemistry. These come mostly from groups developing the products.[4][5][6][10][11]

paras: In skin-care products, horse oil is used as a rich emollient and occlusive-type moisturiser. Users and makers describe it as helping dry, rough or flaky skin look smoother and more supple, and it appears in creams and balms sold in Japan and Korea. Researchers describe it as a long-used ingredient in traditional skin care whose biological effects on skin were only recently examined.[6]
More recent formulations package the oil into dissolving microneedle patches intended for the fine lines around the eyes, where the aim is to deliver the lipid through the outer skin layer.[4][5]

Mid-twentieth-century biochemical studies analysed the fatty acids of horse depot fat, muscle and liver, and compared horse oil with fats from other pasture-fed animals.[2][3] A 2018 study notes it contains unsaturated fatty acids similar to those in human skin and used it as a starting material for producing sophorolipid biosurfactants for cosmetics.[1]

Manufacturing studies have looked at purifying the oil. A 2024 study extracted horse oil from neck fat by supercritical fluid extraction and compared activated carbon, palm activated carbon and zeolite as deodorising agents; zeolite lowered volatile compounds, including a gasoline-like odour component, by more than 90 percent.[12] Other work has examined emulsion stability for cosmetic and food uses and the oxidative stability of horse-oil emulsions with added alpha-tocopherol.[7][13]

A 2019 study in human HaCaT keratinocytes reported that horse oil reduced reactive oxygen species and oxidative damage to lipids, proteins and DNA after UVB exposure, and noted that the oil absorbed light in the UVB range.[6] A 2021 cell study reported that horse oil lowered LPS-induced COX-2 and PGE2 levels in keratinocytes and reduced NF-kappaB translocation, pointing to an anti-inflammatory action in culture.[10] A 2020 mouse study reported that horse oil restored inflammatory gene expression in skin treated with the irritant DNCB.[11]

A 2018 study in Skin Pharmacology and Physiology developed horse-oil-loaded dissolving microneedle patches, confirmed they penetrated pig skin, and ran a 4-week clinical evaluation. The authors reported significant improvements in skin and dermal density, elasticity and moisturisation, with negligible adverse events in a brief safety assessment.[4]

A 2019 study in the Journal of Cosmetic Dermatology tested a patch combining horse oil with adenosine-loaded microneedles on the lateral canthus (outer eye corner) of 20 women. Compared with adenosine-only patches, the combination patches improved skin elasticity, hydration, dermal density and wrinkles, and no adverse events were observed.[5]
Both trials were small and carried out by the groups that developed the patches. A rat study compared horse oil with other oils for cholesterol effects, which concerns diet rather than skin.[8]

The patch studies reported no or negligible adverse events over short periods.[4][5] A 2025 analytical study developed a deep-learning infrared-spectroscopy method to detect adulteration, stating that fraud is common in the horse oil market and that heavy adulteration may pose skin and health risks.[9] Researchers therefore treat the authenticity of commercial products as an active concern. As an animal-derived ingredient, it is not suited to people who avoid animal products.

card.summary: An animal-derived emollient oil from Japanese and Korean skin care, backed by small formulation and cell studies only.
card.note: Studies are small and mostly by developers; no independent human trials found.

quick.overview:
Horse oil is a fat from horses used as an emollient in some Japanese and Korean skin-care products. Makers point to its fatty acids resembling those in human skin.
Research is limited to small formulation, cell and patch studies; no independent clinical trial was found.
quick.mechanism: It acts as an emollient supplying unsaturated fatty acids; lab work reports barrier-supporting and antioxidant effects in cultured keratinocytes.
quick.risks: No safety data specific to people were found. It is an animal-derived product, and researchers have studied methods for detecting adulterated oil.
